summary: Defines the Call Processing Language, a simple, extensible language for describing and controlling Internet telephony services. It is designed to run on servers or user agents, be easy for graphical tools to edit, and be independent of signaling protocol.

eli5.summary: It is a way to write simple call rules, such as "if my boss calls, ring me." Even a drawing program could produce the rules.

questions: how to script sip call handling
what is cpl call processing language

why is cpl not turing complete
subtitle: A deliberately limited XML language for describing what a server does with your phone calls.

tldr.problem: Users want to control how their Internet telephony calls are handled (forward, screen, send to voicemail), but a server cannot safely run arbitrary user programs.
tldr.mechanism: CPL scripts are XML trees of nodes and outputs: switches that decide, location nodes that build a set of destinations, and operations such as proxy, redirect and reject. There are no variables, loops or recursion, so every script ends.
tldr.outcome: A server can accept user-supplied scripts, check them when they are uploaded, and run them with bounded cost. Moving scripts between client and server is left to other documents.

today: RFC 3880 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of CPL, with its XML namespace fixed and enhancements required to come as extensions.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Call Processing Language (CPL) describes and controls Internet telephony services. It is not tied to one signalling protocol; the RFC expects it to be used with both the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP, RFC 3261) and H.323.

CPL is powerful enough to describe many services but is limited so it can run safely in telephony servers. It is not Turing-complete and offers no loops or recursion. It is based on XML, so parsing is easy and graphical tools can create and edit scripts. The framework and requirements are in RFC 2824. This document focuses on servers, and it does not describe how scripts are transported between clients and servers.
sections.eli5: CPL lets you write rules for your phone calls in a safe, simple way. It is like a recipe card that can only say a few things, so it cannot burn the kitchen down.

sections.title: Script Structure and the Location Model
sections.content:
A script holds ancillary information (none is defined yet) and call processing actions. There are two kinds of action. Top-level actions run when a signalling event arrives: incoming for calls whose destination is the script owner, and outgoing for calls whose originator is the script owner. Subactions can be called from other actions but never recursively.

An action is a tree of nodes (decisions or operations) joined by outputs. The server runs the root node, follows one output, and continues until it reaches a node with no specified output. Because the graph is acyclic, this takes a bounded and predictable number of steps. If an output points nowhere, the server falls back to default behavior.

The set of places a call should go is kept as an implicit global location set rather than as node parameters. For incoming it starts empty; for outgoing it starts as the call's destination address.
sections.eli5: Think of a board game path: you stand on a square, the square tells you which way to go next, and you can never walk in a circle. There is also a list of places the call might go, which starts empty for calls coming to you.

sections.title: Switches: Making Decisions
sections.content:
Switches pick an output based on the call. Conditions are tried in order and the first match wins. Every switch can have a not-present output (the value was absent from the request) and an otherwise output, which MUST come last. If nothing matches, default behavior applies.

Five switches are defined. address-switch looks at the origin, destination or original destination, optionally at a subfield (address-type, user, host, port, tel, display), using is, contains or subdomain-of. string-switch checks subject, organization, user-agent or display, comparing as case-insensitive Unicode. language-switch matches the caller's language ranges. time-switch uses recurrence rules borrowed from iCalendar (RFC 2445), with an optional tzid time zone. priority-switch compares against emergency, urgent, normal and non-urgent, and a missing priority counts as normal.

For SIP, origin maps to the From header, destination to the Request-URI and original destination to the To header. The RFC adds that a recurring time interval must be short enough that consecutive intervals do not overlap.
sections.eli5: A switch is a fork in the road. It asks a question like who is calling or what time it is, and sends you down the first path whose answer fits.

sections.title: Locations and Signalling Operations
sections.content:
Location nodes edit the location set. location adds one URL, with an optional priority from 0.0 to 1.0 (default 1.0) and a clear option. lookup fetches locations from a source: a URI that returns a text/uri-list object, or the non-URI source registration, which means the locations registered with the server. Its timeout defaults to 30 seconds and it has success, notfound and failure outputs. remove-location removes one location, or all if none is named.

Signalling operations act on the call. proxy forwards the call to the locations, with outputs busy, noanswer, redirection, failure and default. Its timeout defaults to 20 seconds when a noanswer or default output exists, recurse defaults to yes, and ordering is parallel (the default), sequential or first-only. redirect tells the caller to try the locations itself and has a permanent option. reject ends the call with a status such as busy, notfound, reject or error, and an optional reason. Redirect and reject end the script.
sections.eli5: First you write down who to try calling. Then you choose what to do: ring them all at once, ring them one by one, tell the caller to call someone else, or politely say no.

sections.title: Non-signalling Operations, Subactions and Defaults
sections.content:
Two nodes do not touch the signalling protocol. mail sends an email to a mailto URL, and log records the call to a named log, which is a logical name that servers SHOULD NOT map straight onto file names for security reasons.

Subactions let several outputs share one subtree. A subaction has a unique id and is called with a sub tag using ref. A sub MUST refer only to a subaction defined earlier in the script, which forbids recursion, and servers MUST verify this when a script is submitted.

When an output is left unspecified, the server uses default behavior: with no changes made it behaves as if there were no script; after location changes it proxies or redirects to the location set, or returns a notfound rejection if the set is empty; after a proxy it returns the best response.
sections.eli5: A subaction is a shortcut you can reuse, like a note that says go to the voicemail page. You can only point back to pages already written, so you never go around in circles.

sections.title: Extensions and Registrations
sections.content:
Servers MAY support extra features, identified by XML namespaces. An extension MUST use its own namespace, different from the CPL one, and MUST NOT change the syntax or semantics of the base schema. A server MUST reject any script that uses a namespace it does not understand, or an extension tag that is not properly namespaced.

IANA registered the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:cpl, an XML schema, and the media type application/cpl+xml. The namespace refers only to this version of CPL and will not change; enhancements must come as extensions with different namespaces. Appendix B suggests how CPL maps onto H.323, and Appendix C holds the full XML schema.
sections.eli5: If someone wants to add new kinds of rules, they must label them with their own name tag so the server knows they are extras. If the server does not know the label, it refuses the script instead of guessing.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives eleven example scripts. The call forward busy/no answer script tries one address, and if the call is busy or unanswered within 8 seconds, runs a shared voicemail subaction that proxies to a voicemail address.

Other examples cover unconditional redirect, screening out calls from the user anonymous with a reject, priority and language routing, time-of-day routing, location filtering, and non-signalling operations.
sections.eli5: The examples are like sample recipes: ring my phone, and if I am busy or do not answer, send the caller to voicemail.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
CPL is designed so hostile or misconfigured scripts cannot launch attacks, including denial of service. Runtime is strictly bounded by acyclicity and the set of operations is small, so scripts should not be able to damage a server.

Scripts can redirect people's calls, so the method that carries a script from client to server MUST be strongly authenticated. That method is not specified in the RFC. Servers SHOULD let administrators control which CPL operations are permitted.
sections.eli5: Because the rules are so limited, a bad rule cannot break the phone system. But you must prove who you are before changing your rules, or a stranger could send your calls away.

data.title: Forward to voicemail on busy or no answer
data.code:
<cpl xmlns="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:cpl">
  <subaction id="voicemail">
    <location url="sip:jones@voicemail.example.com">
      <proxy/>
    </location>
  </subaction>
  <incoming>
    <location url="sip:jones@jonespc.example.com">
      <proxy timeout="8">
        <busy><sub ref="voicemail"/></busy>
        <noanswer><sub ref="voicemail"/></noanswer>
      </proxy>
    </location>
  </incoming>
</cpl>
